newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel denies it killed Lebanese shepherd.
newsitem.headline: Israel denies it killed Lebanese shepherd.

text.p: The Israeli army denied that shelling from its forces or those of an allied militia killed a Lebanese shepherd in south Lebanon on Thursday.
Security sources in Lebanon said Khodor Shehadeh, 23, was killed when shells slammed near the village of Froun just north of a south Lebanon zone occupied by Israeli forces.

Sources with the Israeli-backed South Lebanon Army militia (SLA), which patrols the zone, said at about the same time guerrillas fired mortar bombs and anti-tank rockets at a post manned by the militiamen at Shoumariyeh on the edge of the zone facing Froun.

"After checks, we found it impossible a Lebanese citizen could have been hit by fire which Israeli army forces shot in response to terrorist fire that was directed towards an SLA outpost," an Israeli military spokeswoman said.
"The Israeli army returned artillery fire only towards the sources of fire and we emphasise nothing was shot in the area of Froun village," she said.
In reply to a question, the spokeswoman also denied the SLA had fired towards Froun.
Earlier on Thursday, guerrillas attacked another SLA post at Toumat Niha in another sector of the south.
On Tuesday, a civilian woman was killed by Israeli shelling after guerrillas shelled three SLA posts in the zone.
Lebanon has complained over Tuesday's killing to a five-nation committee monitoring a U.S.-brokered south Lebanon ceasefire agreement that bars both sides from targeting civilians.

The ceasefire monitors from the United States, France, Lebanon, Syria and Israel began a meeting on Wednesday to discuss the Lebanese complaint and are still in session at U.N. peacekeepers' headquarters in Naqoura in the south Lebanon zone.

The pro-Iranian Hizbollah (Party of God) leads a guerrilla war on Israeli and SLA forces in a bid to oust them from the 15-km (nine-miles) -deep south Lebanon zone set up in 1985 to prevent cross-border attacks on northern Israel.
